wound.title: Headline later contested with administrative payroll data (Neumark-Wascher 2000 vs Card-Krueger 2000)
wound.detail: The phone-survey FTE measure behind the 13% DiD was directly challenged. Neumark and Wascher (2000, AER 90(5):1362, doi 10.1257/aer.90.5.1362; NBER w5224, 1995) used payroll records from a partly overlapping set of NJ/PA restaurants and found relative employment declines in NJ, which they attributed to measurement error in the survey. Card and Krueger (2000, AER 90(5):1397, doi 10.1257/aer.90.5.1397) replied with BLS ES-202 administrative data. They found small, mostly insignificant effects, which reject the large negative effect but do not reproduce a 13% gain. They also pointed out that the N-W sample was assembled non-randomly through an industry lobbyist. The literature has since moved to "no detectable negative effect" (e.g. Dube et al., Manning 2021 JEP "elusive employment effect"), not a sizeable positive one. So the 13% point estimate (t=2.03) is fragile to the measurement source. The defensible reading is a null that rejects the large-negative prediction.
wound.quote: Relative to stores in Pennsylvania, fast food restaurants in New Jersey increased employment by 13 percent.
wound.remedy: Report the effect as "no evidence of decline" rather than a 13% increase, and note the survey-measurement sensitivity shown by later administrative-data comparisons.

**palimpsestus**
- **Published version found:** I got the AER 1994 paper from davidcard.berkeley.edu, saved it, and ran `compare_versions` against `paper.txt`. Most of the tool's flagged diffs are noise from the two-column layout, so I checked the key passages by hand.

The sample is still 410 stores with an 87% response rate. The McDonald's table (Table 8) and the Interpretation section are kept in both.
- **What changed goes against the headline, not for it:**
  - The CPS teen table (WP Table 9) was moved out of the AER, which refers back to the WP for it. The AER adds that "the standard error is too large (3.2 percent) to allow any confident assessment." The WP had said this evidence "lends further credence".
  - The abstract went from "increased employment by 13 percent" to "no indication that the rise ... reduced employment".
  - "increased" became "may have increased", and "profit-maximizing" became "perfectly competitive".
- **Recorded:**
  - Wound palimpsestus-b8ff3d96 (low, confidence 0.8): the WP oversold the CPS corroboration, and the authors themselves pulled back from it in the AER.
  - A parry: no undisclosed change favours the headline, and there is no pre-registration (the study was fielded in 1992).

**bibliotheca**
- **Wound bibliotheca-5ab6d3d6 (medium, confidence 0.6):** the 13% gain was later contested.
  - Neumark & Wascher (2000 AER, doi 10.1257/aer.90.5.1362) used payroll records and found relative NJ employment declines.
  - Card & Krueger's 2000 reply used BLS ES-202 data and found small, mostly insignificant effects. That rules out a large negative effect but does not reproduce a 13% gain.
  - Later literature (e.g. Manning 2021 JEP) settles on "no detectable negative effect", not a large positive one.
- **Wound bibliotheca-47e1ca10 (low, confidence 0.55):** citation slips.
  - Wellington's own abstract (via OpenAlex) says "less than 1 percent", which is an elasticity of about -0.06. The paper's "0.06 percentage points" looks like the wrong units, understating the effect about fourfold.

events.field: Labor economics: minimum wage employment effects
events.setting: Franchised fast-food restaurants (BK, KFC, Wendy's, Roy Rogers; McDonald's excluded) in New Jersey vs eastern Pennsylvania, Feb-Mar 1992 vs Nov-Dec 1992; NJ minimum rose $4.25 -> $5.05 on 1 April 1992 (+18.8%), legislated in early 1990.
actors: Store managers/franchisees: set staffing schedules weekly; adjust hours, part-time headcount, and menu prices
Franchisors: set pricing guidance and staffing standards (labor-to-sales ratios)
Teen and young adult workers: high turnover (often >100%/yr), mostly part-time
NJ legislature/governor: last-minute attempt to phase the increase was vetoed in March 1992
Survey interviewer/respondents: one phone respondent (often an assistant manager) answering headcount questions

parry.note: Reverse causality is implausible here. The treatment is a statewide wage floor legislated in 1990, two years before the outcome window. Individual stores did not choose it, and 1992 store staffing could not have caused it. The legislature's last-minute attempt to soften the increase failed for reasons unrelated to fast-food hiring. The one timing caveat is anticipation: stores had known about the increase since 1990 and could have adjusted before Wave 1. That would bias the estimate toward zero, not produce a positive effect.
parry.quote: The increase had been legislated two years earlier when the state economy was relatively healthy

parry.note: The paper sets up the competitive model's predictions fairly: employment falls and prices rise, with a quantified prediction of -0.4 to -1.0 FTE per store from Brown-Gilroy-Kohen. It also tests the distinctive predictions of the monopsony alternative (prices should fall; employment should rise most at the lowest-wage stores and at bonus-paying, supply-constrained stores). The authors admit that their own price evidence contradicts monopsony and that the recruitment-bonus test fails. They do not borrow a theory whose assumptions fail and then present it as confirmed. The conclusion says both mo
parry.quote: Although monopsonistic models provide a potential explanation for the observed employment effects of the New Jersey minimum wage, they cannot explain the observed price effects.

wound.title: Service-quality and menu-mix stories added only after the price evidence contradicted monopsony
wound.detail: The data show employment rising and prices rising, which fits neither the competitive model nor monopsony. Instead of treating this as a sign that the employment estimate may be noise, the paper adds two untested auxiliary mechanisms after the fact: variable service quality and relative menu-price changes, the latter supported only by an 8% entree vs -1.5% fries/soda comparison with no standard errors. Neither is measured or tested. A simpler account is that the true employment effect is near zero and the +2.76 FTE estimate is mostly sampling and measurement noise. That account explains the price rise, the zero within-NJ price gradient, and the failed bonus test without new machinery. The authors are candid that these ideas are speculative, so the severity is low.
wound.quote: The strict link between the employment and price effects of a rise in the minimum wage may be tempered if fast food stores can vary the quality of service
wound.remedy: Present these mechanisms as untested conjectures. Give the plain reading that the employment effect is near zero and imprecise equal weight.

wound.title: The NJ effect is carried by five Pennsylvania stores; the median effect is 1.0 FTE and insignificant
wound.detail: The paper never checks outliers or influence. In the Table 4 sample (n=357, only 67 PA stores), dropping the single most influential store, PA sheet 445, cuts the NJ coefficient from 2.30 to 1.70. That store reports 70.5 FTE (50 full-time, 35 part-time) with 3 cash registers, more than three times the sample mean, and 29 FTE in wave 2. Dropping the top 3 influential stores gives 0.94; dropping 5 gives 0.34 (p=0.78). All of them are large PA stores reporting drops of 18-42 FTE. A median regression gives 1.00 (SE 1.04, p=0.34). Trimming the top and bottom 5% of changes gives 0.68 (p=0.48). Excluding stores with 50 or more FTE in wave 1 gives 1.31 (p=0.30). The 'relative gain' is a fall in the PA mean driven by a few very large PA stores whose wave-1 counts look implausible relative to their size, not a broad shift across NJ stores. Innocent explanation: these could be real large stores that cut staff; the paper gives no way to tell.
wound.remedy: Report median and trimmed estimates and leave-one-out influence. Verify the largest PA stores' counts against payroll records.

wound.detail: Table 4 reports conventional OLS standard errors (2.33, SE 1.19, p=0.052). The PA employment changes have 1.39 times the SD of NJ's (11.3 vs 8.1), and PA is the small group (67 vs 290 stores), so the homoskedastic SE understates uncertainty. wound.title: The whole effect is a fall in PA full-time headcount, and phone-reported FT/PT splits are unstable
wound.detail: FTE counts a full-time worker as 1 and a part-timer as 0.5, so if a respondent relabels workers between the two categories, FTE moves without any change in labor. In the data, the NJ-PA gain comes entirely from full-time counts: full-time change NJ coefficient +2.52, part-time -0.36, managers -0.04. PA stores report an average full-time fall of 2.18 with part-time flat. 43 of 357 stores (16 of 67 in PA, 24%; 27 of 290 in NJ, 9%) show a full-time change of 15 or more workers with an opposite-sign part-time change, e.g. PA sheet 441: 30 FT/10 PT to 0 FT/30 PT; sheet 56: 20/20 to 0/36. The share of PA stores reporting zero full-time workers doubles from 10.4% to 20.9%. The authors' own reliability ratio for FTE is only 0.70. Total-headcount and log-employment versions show no significant effect: headcount +2.12 (p=0.19), log change -0.011 (p=0.79). Payroll records (Neumark & Wascher 2000, AER 90(5)) found the opposite sign. Innocent explanation: real reclassification of workers during a recession; it cannot be ruled out without hours data, which the survey did not collect.
wound.quote: Full-time equivalent employment is defined as the number of full-time workers (including managers) plus 0.5 times the number of part-time workers.
wound.remedy: Use payroll hours (as in the later ES-202 / payroll comparisons). Report headcount and log outcomes alongside FTE. Flag stores with FT/PT swaps for re-contact.

wound.title: One pre-period, 67-79 control stores, and a dose-response that vanishes within regions
wound.detail: Identification rests on parallel trends between NJ and eastern PA over Feb-Nov 1992. With one pre-period there is no way to test pre-trends. The control group is small (79 stores, 67 in the regression), surveyed with fewer callbacks, and its mean is moved by a handful of large stores (see scutum). The within-NJ high-wage placebo (-0.34 vs PA, SE 1.66 on 67 high-wage stores) is underpowered: it could not distinguish a 2-3 FTE gap. That it 'clearly passes' is a failure to reject, not evidence of validity. The paper's stronger test, GAP with region dummies, is insignificant (11.91, SE 7.39), and the authors note this. Within NJ alone, GAP is 12.2 (p=0.085) and falls to 4.5 (p=0.51) once wave-1 employment enters by OLS, because higher-gap NJ stores started smaller and the change regresses on initial size. The authors' IV for wave-1 size (registers) has a first-stage F of about 9 and a wide CI. NJ's recession was worse than PA's, which helps the authors, but a PA-specific shock among large stores is not ruled out.

events.text:
**Fragility score 60.4, "Mortally wounded."** New Jersey's 1992 minimum-wage rise did not visibly cost fast-food jobs, but the paper's headline "13 percent" employment gain does not hold up.

I reproduced Tables 3 and 4 exactly from the authors' own survey file and SAS program (NJ dummy 2.33 vs their 2.33; standard error 1.19). I found no sign of fabricated data and no arithmetic contradictions, only a few wrong table cross-references. The problem is how fragile the positive result is.

**The three deepest wounds**

1. **Five Pennsylvania stores carry the result** (Table 4, cols 1–2). Abstract: *"Relative to stores in Pennsylvania, fast food restaurants in New Jersey increased employment by 13 percent."*
   - One PA store reports 70.5 full-time-equivalent workers on 3 cash registers in wave 1, about three times the average store, and 29 in wave 2. Dropping it cuts the effect from 2.30 to 1.70.
   - Dropping five large PA stores leaves 0.34 (p=0.78).
   - The median-store effect is 1.0 (p=0.34).
   - The "gain" is really a fall in the mean of a small control group (67 stores).

2. **The effect is entirely in full-time counts, which are unreliable.** The paper says: *"Full-time equivalent employment is defined as the number of full-time workers (including managers) plus 0.5 times the number of part-time workers."*
   - Full-time counts give +2.52; part-time −0.36; managers about 0.
   - 43 stores (24% of PA stores) report swapping 15 or more workers between full-time and part-time. For example, one goes from 30 full-time/10 part-time to 0/30. The share of PA stores reporting no full-time workers doubles.
   - The authors' own reliability ratio for this employment measure is only 0.70. Later payroll records (Neumark & Wascher 2000) found the opposite sign.

3. **Significance depends on how uncertainty is measured.** The paper uses standard errors that assume both states' stores are equally variable, but PA's are about 40% more variable.
   - With standard errors that allow for this, the NJ effect has p=0.11; a bootstrap gives p=0.13.
   - On a per-store percentage or log scale, the effect is about 5% and never significant.
   - The paper's own text concedes that with region controls it is *"no longer possible to reject the null hypothesis of a 0 employment effect of the minimum wage."*
   - In my run of 1,008 alternative specifications, only 7.7% are positive and significant at 5%. In the arsenal's 384-specification run, none are.

**What survived:** the sign. 98% of specifications are positive and none is significantly negative, so the data do rule out the large job losses the standard model predicts. That narrower claim, "no indication that the rise reduced employment", is what the authors themselves wrote in the 1994 AER version.

**One correction:** two recorded wounds (fucus and mundus) cite a log-employment change of −0.011. That number came from a bug in my own script, which I've fixed. The correct figure is +0.056 (p=0.28), and I recorded the correction in the report. The wounds still stand in weaker form: the per-store effect is positive but insignificant, not zero.

**What would change my mind:** payroll or hours records for the same stores showing a similar relative gain in New Jersey; confirmation that the large PA stores' wave-1 counts are real; or employment data from before 1992 showing NJ and PA were on parallel trends.

The full report is `tabula.html` in the case folder. The scripts are in `code/` and their outputs in `out/`.

wounds.title: The NJ effect is carried by five Pennsylvania stores; the median effect is 1.0 FTE and insignificant
wounds.detail: The paper never checks outliers or influence. In the Table 4 sample (n=357, only 67 PA stores), dropping the single most influential store, PA sheet 445, cuts the NJ coefficient from 2.30 to 1.70. That store reports 70.5 FTE (50 full-time, 35 part-time) with 3 cash registers, more than three times the sample mean, and 29 FTE in wave 2. Dropping the top 3 influential stores gives 0.94; dropping 5 gives 0.34 (p=0.78). All of them are large PA stores reporting drops of 18-42 FTE. A median regression gives 1.00 (SE 1.04, p=0.34). Trimming the top and bottom 5% of changes gives 0.68 (p=0.48). Excluding stores with 50 or more FTE in wave 1 gives 1.31 (p=0.30). The 'relative gain' is a fall in the PA mean driven by a few very large PA stores whose wave-1 counts look implausible relative to their size, not a broad shift across NJ stores. Innocent explanation: these could be real large stores that cut staff; the paper gives no way to tell.
wounds.remedy: Report median and trimmed estimates and leave-one-out influence. Verify the largest PA stores' counts against payroll records.

wounds.title: The whole effect is a fall in PA full-time headcount, and phone-reported FT/PT splits are unstable
wounds.detail: FTE counts a full-time worker as 1 and a part-timer as 0.5, so if a respondent relabels workers between the two categories, FTE moves without any change in labor. In the data, the NJ-PA gain comes entirely from full-time counts: full-time change NJ coefficient +2.52, part-time -0.36, managers -0.04. PA stores report an average full-time fall of 2.18 with part-time flat. 43 of 357 stores (16 of 67 in PA, 24%; 27 of 290 in NJ, 9%) show a full-time change of 15 or more workers with an opposite-sign part-time change, e.g. PA sheet 441: 30 FT/10 PT to 0 FT/30 PT; sheet 56: 20/20 to 0/36. The share of PA stores reporting zero full-time workers doubles from 10.4% to 20.9%. The authors' own reliability ratio for FTE is only 0.70. Total-headcount and log-employment versions show no significant effect: headcount +2.12 (p=0.19), log change -0.011 (p=0.79). Payroll records (Neumark & Wascher 2000, AER 90(5)) found the opposite sign. Innocent explanation: real reclassification of workers during a recession; it cannot be ruled out without hours data, which the survey did not collect.

wounds.detail: Table 4 reports conventional OLS standard errors (2.33, SE 1.19, p=0.052). The PA employment changes have 1.39 times the SD of NJ's (11.3 vs 8.1), and PA is the small group (67 vs 290 stores), so the homoskedastic SE understates uncertainty. Heteroskedasticity-robust SEs: HC1 1.45 (p=0.11), HC3 1.47 (p=0.12). Wild bootstrap p=0.13; Welch t on the regression sample 1.59. The design cannot reject a zero effect at conventional levels. The paper's own store-level proportional models (Table 4, cols 6-10) give a NJ coefficient of 0.05 (SE 0.05), insignificant. On the same data, the log change in employment for open stores gives -0.011 (SE 0.043). The 13% figure only reappears when proportional changes are weighted by initial employment (Table 5 row 9), i.e. when the large stores whose outliers drive the result get the most weight. wounds.title: Service-quality and menu-mix stories added only after the price evidence contradicted monopsony
wounds.detail: The data show employment rising and prices rising, which fits neither the competitive model nor monopsony. Instead of treating this as a sign that the employment estimate may be noise, the paper adds two untested auxiliary mechanisms after the fact: variable service quality and relative menu-price changes, the latter supported only by an 8% entree vs -1.5% fries/soda comparison with no standard errors. Neither is measured or tested. A simpler account is that the true employment effect is near zero and the +2.76 FTE estimate is mostly sampling and measurement noise. That account explains the price rise, the zero within-NJ price gradient, and the failed bonus test without new machinery. The authors are candid that these ideas are speculative, so the severity is low.

wounds.remedy: Present these mechanisms as untested conjectures. Give the plain reading that the employment effect is near zero and imprecise equal weight.

tabula.final:
**Fragility score 60.4, "Mortally wounded."** New Jersey's 1992 minimum-wage rise did not visibly cost fast-food jobs, but the paper's headline "13 percent" employment gain does not hold up.

I reproduced Tables 3 and 4 exactly from the authors' own survey file and SAS program (NJ dummy 2.33 vs their 2.33; standard error 1.19). I found no sign of fabricated data and no arithmetic contradictions, only a few wrong table cross-references. The problem is how fragile the positive result is.

**The three deepest wounds**

1. **Five Pennsylvania stores carry the result** (Table 4, cols 1–2). Abstract: *"Relative to stores in Pennsylvania, fast food restaurants in New Jersey increased employment by 13 percent."*
   - One PA store reports 70.5 full-time-equivalent workers on 3 cash registers in wave 1, about three times the average store, and 29 in wave 2. Dropping it cuts the effect from 2.30 to 1.70.
   - Dropping five large PA stores leaves 0.34 (p=0.78).
   - The median-store effect is 1.0 (p=0.34).
   - The "gain" is really a fall in the mean of a small control group (67 stores).

2. **The effect is entirely in full-time counts, which are unreliable.** The paper says: *"Full-time equivalent employment is defined as the number of full-time workers (including managers) plus 0.5 times the number of part-time workers."*
   - Full-time counts give +2.52; part-time −0.36; managers about 0.
   - 43 stores (24% of PA stores) report swapping 15 or more workers between full-time and part-time. For example, one goes from 30 full-time/10 part-time to 0/30. The share of PA stores reporting no full-time workers doubles.
   - The authors' own reliability ratio for this employment measure is only 0.70. Later payroll records (Neumark & Wascher 2000) found the opposite sign.

3. **Significance depends on how uncertainty is measured.** The paper uses standard errors that assume both states' stores are equally variable, but PA's are about 40% more variable.
   - With standard errors that allow for this, the NJ effect has p=0.11; a bootstrap gives p=0.13.
   - On a per-store percentage or log scale, the effect is about 5% and never significant.
   - The paper's own text concedes that with region controls it is *"no longer possible to reject the null hypothesis of a 0 employment effect of the minimum wage."*
   - In my run of 1,008 alternative specifications, only 7.7% are positive and significant at 5%. In the arsenal's 384-specification run, none are.

**What survived:** the sign. 98% of specifications are positive and none is significantly negative, so the data do rule out the large job losses the standard model predicts. That narrower claim, "no indication that the rise reduced employment", is what the authors themselves wrote in the 1994 AER version.

**One correction:** two recorded wounds (fucus and mundus) cite a log-employment change of −0.011. That number came from a bug in my own script, which I've fixed. The correct figure is +0.056 (p=0.28), and I recorded the correction in the report. The wounds still stand in weaker form: the per-store effect is positive but insignificant, not zero.

**What would change my mind:** payroll or hours records for the same stores showing a similar relative gain in New Jersey; confirmation that the large PA stores' wave-1 counts are real; or employment data from before 1992 showing NJ and PA were on parallel trends.

field.field: Labor economics: minimum wage employment effects
field.setting: Franchised fast-food restaurants (BK, KFC, Wendy's, Roy Rogers; McDonald's excluded) in New Jersey vs eastern Pennsylvania, Feb-Mar 1992 vs Nov-Dec 1992; NJ minimum rose $4.25 -> $5.05 on 1 April 1992 (+18.8%), legislated in early 1990.
actors: Store managers/franchisees: set staffing schedules weekly; adjust hours, part-time headcount, and menu prices
Franchisors: set pricing guidance and staffing standards (labor-to-sales ratios)
Teen and young adult workers: high turnover (often >100%/yr), mostly part-time
NJ legislature/governor: last-minute attempt to phase the increase was vetoed in March 1992
Survey interviewer/respondents: one phone respondent (often an assistant manager) answering headcount questions
field.claimed_mechanism: Raising the minimum wage did not reduce, and if anything raised, fast-food employment; consistent with monopsony/search frictions (though the authors note prices rose, which monopsony does not predict).
field.real_mechanism: Fast-food staffing responds to sales volume via labor-to-sales targets and adjusts mainly at the hours margin; headcount (what was surveyed) is a noisy proxy for labor input. With very high turnover, a store can shrink or grow headcount within weeks, so an 8-month window is long enough for headcount adjustment but the survey measure (headcount on phone, reliability 0.70 per the authors) is dominated by noise. A recession hitting NJ harder than PA cuts against the finding, which helps the authors.
field.institutions: NJ increase legislated in 1990, so firms could anticipate it for two years (adjustments before Wave 1 would bias toward zero). Wave 1 surveyed one month before the hike, Wave 2 seven to eight months after. PA control: northeast Philadelphia suburbs and Allentown-Easton. No payroll records: phone-reported headcount of full-time, part-time, managers.
field.magnitudes: Mean FTE ~21 per store; PA n=79 vs NJ n=331. Conventional elasticity -0.1 to -0.3 implies -0.4 to -1.0 FTE per store; reported effect +2.76 FTE (+13%), i.e., an implied labor-demand elasticity of about +0.7 w.r.t. the store wage. Labor share ~30% of costs; observed NJ relative price rise ~4%.
field.theory: Competitive labor demand (Stigler 1946) predicts employment falls; monopsony / Burdett-Mortensen wage-posting predicts employment may rise, most at lowest-wage firms, and prices fall.
theory_assumptions: Monopsony requires upward-sloping store-level labor supply: plausible for a single store only in thin local markets, doubtful with many competing low-wage employers in suburban NJ
Monopsony with price-taking output market predicts lower prices, but NJ prices rose ~4% relative
Competitive model with near-constant returns predicts both output and employment fall
rival_explanations: Measurement error in phone-reported headcount (reliability 0.70) plus small PA sample: the DiD is driven by a -2.16 FTE drop in 79 PA stores
Region-specific demand shocks: PA suburbs vs NJ; within-region GAP effect insignificant
Mean reversion: NJ stores started smaller (20.4 vs 23.3) and converged
Payroll records (Neumark-Wascher 2000) show the opposite sign; BLS ES-202 data (Card-Krueger 2000) show roughly zero
sources: Card & Krueger (2000) AER 90(5):1397 reply using BLS ES-202 data
Paper text: NJ unemployment rose more than PA in 1992
